passage:
At two, Pranav hid behind his mother Nandini's legs when the neighbour bent down to say hello. He looked at the floor, said nothing and only peeped out again after ten quiet minutes. Nandini stroked his hair and did not push him to speak.

At nine, Pranav got a spelling test back with red ink all over it. He slid the paper into his bag, went quiet and muttered, "I'm just stupid." Nandini sat beside him that evening. "You got these words wrong today," she said. "That doesn't make you a stupid person. Shall we practise the tricky ones together?" His shoulders dropped a little.

At twenty, Pranav's friend Wasim came back from an interview looking flat. Pranav sat next to him on the hostel steps, did not offer a list of fixes and only said, "That sounds rough. I'm here." After a long time Wasim began talking. When he said things felt heavy every day, Pranav suggested the college counsellor and walked over with him.

qa.q: What did Pranav do when the neighbour bent down to say hello at two?
qa.a: Pranav hid behind his mother Nandini's legs, looked at the floor and said nothing.

qa.q: What connects Pranav hiding at two, feeling stupid at nine and sitting with Wasim at twenty?
qa.a: At two Pranav hides behind Nandini and she does not push him to speak; at nine he mutters that he is stupid and she separates the person from the wrong words; at twenty Pranav sits quietly with Wasim without offering fixes. Each time, calm listening gives safety.

qa.q: What is Pranav feeling when he mutters that he is stupid?
qa.a: Pranav feels ashamed and hurt after the red ink, so he goes quiet and hides the paper in his bag.

qa.q: Why was walking with Wasim to the counsellor a wise step?
qa.a: Wasim said things felt heavy every day, and that is more than a friend's company can fix, so involving the counsellor added professional help.

grounding: Social sensitivity across ages: a shy toddler given time, a child's shame handled by separating the person from the mistake, and a young adult offering steady support to a friend.
